reason: Keep-alive/eviction policy over production FaaS traces is an ideal trace-driven simulation target, but no official repo was found so everything would have to be reimplemented.

Multi-SLO speculative-decoding scheduler is core LLM-serving with a published AE artifact, but the artifact assumes 8x A100 + Docker + CUDA 12.4 (driver here caps at 12.2), so a real port plus scale-down is needed.
In-database neural model selection is ML/DB modeling rather than OS resource management, though it runs on one GPU and the repo is linked.
No abstract, PDF or artifact is public; the title hints at a thread abstraction that could well be kernel-side, so nothing can be judged and it must be scored conservatively.
Memory-access-centric DL compiler evaluated on a single GPU with an artifact branch, but the pinned CUDA/TVM/nnfusion stack is a heavy build for a 10-week project.
A GPU kernel DSL/compiler is only systems-adjacent for an OS course; Ampere is supported and the NVIDIA repo is real, but some features target Blackwell.
Tensor-core GNN kernel work is GPU-kernel engineering rather than OS resource management; single-A5000 reproducible but repo completeness unknown.
KV-cache eviction/recall plus host-memory prefetching is exactly the OS-flavored LLM-serving problem, but the artifact ships as Docker for an 8-GPU server and Docker is unavailable here.
Request-group queue ordering on top of vLLM is a clean scheduling artifact in active Python; a 7B single-GPU scale-down is straightforward and the LP/ordering heuristic is an obvious swap-in surface.
Single-GPU metric-space index fits the machine, but no official repo was located so the GPU tree would have to be written from scratch.
Per-model scheduling of diffusion workflows is a good serving-systems topic, but no artifact exists and the per-model scaling / adaptive parallelism claims are cluster-scale.
Fork plus soft-dirty snapshot/restore is genuinely user-space and benchmarkable standalone, but the end-to-end OpenWhisk+Docker harness cannot run here and the artifact is only a Zenodo record.
Federated client-selection and staleness policies are ML-training policy work rather than OS resource management, though the FedScale-style simulator runs fine on one node.
CPU-only storage compression for ingestion pipelines fits the machine perfectly; the clustering heuristic is swappable, but artifact completeness is unverified.

Hot/cold neuron-aware GPU-CPU hybrid offloading designed for exactly this one-consumer-GPU-plus-large-RAM machine, llama.cpp-based user-space build with a mature repo and obvious policy-tuning hypotheses.
Single-GPU DL compiler whose headline numbers use a 3B model that fits 24 GB, with a rich pass-level improvement surface; risk is the polyhedral/LLVM toolchain build under $HOME.
Carbon-aware retraining scheduling is only loosely an OS problem, depends on external carbon traces and edge-server assumptions, and no code was found.
LSM growth policy is a textbook storage-engine topic that runs on one NVMe, but no repo was located so the prototype key-value store would need reimplementation.
GPU Datalog for neurosymbolic programming is a language/runtime contribution far from OS resource management, though it is user-space and single-GPU.

Cache eviction with released code, pre-trained model, libCacheSim/CacheLib integrations and thousands of public traces; pure trace-driven simulation with an open space of policy and parameter-learning variants.
Cooperative compilation plus scheduling for model serving is a reasonable single-GPU topic, but no code has been released so there is nothing to build on.
The headline metric is model confidentiality rather than a resource-management win, and validating preserved optimization quality means GPU-hour-heavy autotuning.
ANN index framework runs comfortably on one machine but is an algorithms/data-structures contribution rather than an OS systems-resource problem.
A vision-track paper whose prototype runtime is likely early-stage, so there is no solid baseline to improve on within ten weeks.
KV-cache reuse across fine-tuned variants is a great single-GPU 8B-scale topic with clear layer-selection knobs, but no artifact URL exists so the release is unconfirmed.
A DRAM-only variant ships in the repo and hash-index memory/latency tradeoffs suit the course, but the paper's best results need Optane PMEM and AVX-512 that this Zen3 machine lacks.
Out-of-core single-machine graph engine has real I/O and buffering behavior to study, but the contribution is a graph-processing programming model more than OS resource management.
CPU-side grammar compilation overlapped with GPU decode is a genuine CPU/GPU pipelining problem, the engine is widely deployed with easy baselines, and it runs on any single GPU.
Decoupling LSM flush/compaction to kill write stalls is core storage-engine work with a RocksDB+YCSB artifact, but the Optane fast tier is unavailable so the hybrid setup must be emulated.
Early-exit ramps bolted onto a serving runtime are pure user-space PyTorch with models that fit 24 GB; the multi-GPU cluster evaluation needs a single-GPU trace replay and goodput numbers will shift.
Multi-tenant SSD virtualization is a good storage topic, but there is no official repo and the evaluation likely needs an SSD emulator that would have to be stood up first.
Causal configuration tuning is an ML-for-systems method; offline datasets keep it runnable, but the original Jetson target hardware is absent so live experiments must be redesigned.

An on-GPU KV allocator that compacts fragmented free lists is memory management in the purest OS sense, single-GPU vLLM-style, and an ideal target for a better-allocator or better-compression hypothesis; only CUDA-toolkit versioning is a risk.
Application-aware retraining of neural networks is model customization rather than systems resource management, though it is single-GPU and needs no root.
A learned counting/cardinality structure sits in DB-ML territory with little OS content, and no artifact was found.
A mature FL platform that simulates clients on one node, but it is framework/ML infrastructure rather than an OS resource-management result to improve.
Tensor-core SpMM kernel optimization is low-level GPU kernel engineering; Ampere supports cp.async but the larger graphs must be trimmed from 80 GB to 24 GB.
Model-fusion graph search is an ML-model transformation, and the repeated fine-tuning search phase is GPU-hour heavy for a ten-week budget on one card.
A fault-injection testing tool is bug-finding rather than resource management, and reproducing results needs a .NET toolchain under $HOME plus cloud emulators.
CPU-only storage-engine compression is a clean fit for the machine; the repo is linked but its completeness and data availability are unverified.

Tiering and auto-scaling policies are attractive to redesign, but the evaluated stack is a distributed AWS deployment pulling in Zookeeper, BookKeeper and S3, so the single-node scale-down is a large risky lift.
An RL-built trajectory index is a specialized spatial-DB result with no located artifact and little OS-resource content.
The released artifact is only a pseudo-quantization/perplexity workflow; the actual speedup rests on a hardware unit that cannot be built here, leaving no performance hypothesis to test.
Explicitly unprivileged sandboxing on user namespaces and overlay mounts, which this machine supports, with a public repo and a clean effect-capture/commit overhead target to optimize.
A Postgres extension for dynamic model slicing is in-database ML serving; runnable on one GPU but far from an OS resource-management hypothesis.
Query-aware cascade and scheduling logic is user-space Python and SD-class models fit 24 GB; the multi-GPU resource-allocation experiments are the part that must be scaled down or simulated.
Feature compression co-designed with a GPU cache touches caching and data-loading pipelines and has a single-GPU config, but the framing is GNN training throughput.
Dependency tracking plus intermediate-result caching is entirely user-space on one machine, with natural improvement axes in caching policy and dependency granularity.
An optimal buffer-replacement policy for out-of-core computation is a textbook caching/eviction problem that runs on one node; repo completeness is the only unknown.
Much of the contribution is at the cryptographic-protocol level, which is outside an OS course's core, and the artifact is only a Zenodo record.
Compressed log storage with an FM-index is a solid storage topic and a local MinIO or filesystem backend substitutes for S3, though that substitution changes the I/O regime the design targets.
Disk-resident learned indexes on a single NVMe in user space fit the machine exactly, and the I/O-aware design choices give plenty of well-defined variants to test.

Cache sizing and admission with a separately released trace-driven simulator is exactly the single-machine evaluation path this project needs; cost parameters must come from the paper and the repos lack READMEs so build effort is unverified.
Resizable fingerprint filters are a small CPU-only data structure that would run anywhere, but no repo was located so it would be a from-scratch implementation.
